title: The evaluation pyramid
point: Many cheap deterministic checks at the base, fewer scenario and trajectory evals in the middle, and a few expensive end-to-end judgements at the top, each run at its own cadence.
definition: The evaluation pyramid layers agent tests by cost and scope. A wide base of deterministic checks runs on every commit. A middle of scenario and trajectory evals checks the steps taken, and a narrow top of human or model-judged reviews runs less often.

objective.text: Given a list of agent checks, place each in the right layer of the pyramid and state how often it should run.

misconceptions.claim: End-to-end judgements are the only evals that matter, because users see only the final answer.
misconceptions.correction: End-to-end judgements are slow and costly, so they run rarely and find failures late. Cheap base checks catch broken schemas and loop bounds on every commit, minutes after the change.

misconceptions.claim: If the final answer is right, the trajectory does not need testing.
misconceptions.correction: A right answer can hide a wrong path, such as an unneeded refund call or ten wasted steps. Trajectory evals catch unsafe or costly behaviour that the answer alone conceals.

l1: The base holds deterministic checks: schema validity, tool-contract tests and unit tests of loop bounds. They are cheap, fast and exact, so they run on every commit.
The middle holds scenario and trajectory evals. A scripted task checks whether the agent took sensible steps and called the right tools in a sensible order.
The top holds end-to-end judgements by humans or a model judge. They are expensive and slow, so they run on release candidates rather than on every change.
l2: Take a support agent with 400 base checks, 120 scenarios and a 300-item judged set. The base runs in about two minutes and costs nothing beyond compute.
The 120 scenarios replay recorded tool responses, so they need no live systems and finish in about ten minutes. They run on every merge to the main branch.
The judged set needs 300 model-judge calls plus a human sample of 50 conversations. It runs nightly and before each release, because a full pass costs real money and an afternoon of review.
l3: The shape follows cost per finding. A schema check costs a fraction of a cent and fails loudly, while a human review costs minutes per item and finds subtle problems.
When a failure first shows up at the top, push a cheaper test down the pyramid. A judged failure caused by a malformed date becomes a base schema check that runs on every commit.
An inverted pyramid, with most effort in manual review, is slow and leaves regressions undetected between reviews. Teams then ship less often, or ship without evidence.
